questions.q: Why does the lesson argue a reading log matters more than simply reading more papers?
options: Because logs are required for academic credit
Because the lasting value is in your own compressed judgment of a paper, which you'll otherwise forget
Because reading logs are the only way to track page counts
Because more papers read always means better understanding
questions.explain: The specifics of a paper fade from memory, but a written record of the load-bearing claim and your judgment of the evidence preserves the part that's actually useful later.

questions.q: What is the benefit of revisiting a paper on a spaced schedule rather than reading it only once?
options: It satisfies a citation requirement
New context accumulated since the first read often reveals things that were missed the first time
It guarantees the paper's results will reproduce
It is required before citing the paper in your own work
questions.explain: Because understanding decays and context grows over time, a later revisit — especially of foundational papers — can surface insights the first pass missed.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what do reading groups add that solo reading typically can't?
options: A guarantee that the paper's main claim is correct
A deadline that forces completion, plus outside objections to claims you might accept too easily
Faster reading speed
Automatic reproduction of the paper's results
questions.explain: Explaining a paper to colleagues who push back on claims is one of the fastest ways to discover you missed or misjudged the load-bearing claim.

questions.q: What approach does the lesson recommend for staying current with the ML literature?
options: Reading every paper posted to arXiv each day
Following a small, deliberately chosen set of sources on a fixed cadence rather than attempting comprehensive coverage
Only reading papers that go viral on social media
Reading exclusively papers from one's own employer
questions.explain: Comprehensive coverage of the literature isn't feasible, so the lesson recommends curating a small set of trusted sources and checking them on a fixed cadence.

questions.q: What does the lesson say about skipping a paper you never got around to reading?
options: It means your reading practice has failed
It's a completely normal and expected outcome, not a failure
It should never happen if you triage correctly
It only happens to inexperienced researchers
questions.explain: A sustainable reading practice treats 'I didn't read that one' as normal, since trying to read everything leads to shallow reading or burnout rather than better understanding.
